subject: Social Science
central_question: How are economic activities classified into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors, and why are the three sectors interdependent?
in_scope_units: Introduction — growth and diversity of economic activities and the need for classification
The Classification of Economic Activities into Economic Sectors — common characteristics and three broad sectors
Primary activities — direct dependence on nature and extraction of raw materials
Secondary activities — construction, utilities and transformation of raw materials into products
Tertiary activities — services supporting people, production, trade and everyday life
Interdependence Among Sectors — natural materials, processing, transport, trade and final consumption
Dairy cooperative: from farm to plate — AMUL, farmers, middlemen, cooperation, processing and distribution
Book production — pulp, paper, printing, transport and the three-sector chain
Paper recycling — saving trees, landfill space, energy and water
Neighbourhood activity mapping — classification, links and consequences if one activity stops
banned_topics: Economic and non-economic activity classification from Chapter 13 except as introductory background
Advanced industrial policy or international trade theory

known_pitfalls.claim: The primary sector is the most important, so the other sectors are optional.
known_pitfalls.correction: All three sectors support one another and are needed to move goods from raw material to final use.

known_pitfalls.claim: The tertiary sector produces no value because it provides services rather than goods.
known_pitfalls.correction: Transport, banking, communication, healthcare, repair and retail are essential economic services.

known_pitfalls.claim: A factory that processes milk belongs to the primary sector because milk comes from animals.
known_pitfalls.correction: Milking livestock is primary; processing milk into butter, cheese or powder is secondary.

recommended_example_progression: Sort listed activities into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors using a classification chart.
Connect natural resources with extraction or cultivation in the primary sector.
Use examples of grain to flour, wood to furniture and cotton to clothing for the secondary sector.
Trace all three sectors and cooperative action using the AMUL 'farm to plate' story.
Build flow diagrams of sector interdependence.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: Refer to the chapter-end 'Questions, activities and projects' Questions 1-3 on page 208.
